course.title: Growth Hacking
course.description: Growth hacking is the discipline of finding fast, cheap, experiment-driven ways to grow a product's user base and revenue. This course walks through the AARRR funnel, the growth experiment loop, acquisition channels, viral loops and referrals, activation and retention, product-led growth, and the ethics and limits of growth tactics. The structure is adapted from the Growth hacking article on Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: The term growth hacking was coined by...
questions.explanation: Sean Ellis coined the phrase in 2010 to name a role whose single goal is growth.

questions.prompt: In the AARRR funnel, the first A stands for...
questions.explanation: The stages are Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue - see 'The AARRR funnel'.

questions.prompt: A viral coefficient greater than one means...
options: each user brings on average more than one new user
questions.explanation: When each user brings more than one new user, the base grows on its own, cohort after cohort.

questions.prompt: The north-star metric is best described as...
options: the single metric that best captures the value the product delivers
questions.explanation: A good north-star reflects real delivered value and predicts long-term growth.

questions.prompt: In an A/B test, the control group...
options: sees the existing version, as a baseline for comparison
questions.explanation: The control is the unchanged version you measure the variant against.

options: a user reaching a first moment of real value
questions.explanation: Activation is the 'aha' moment when a new user first experiences the product's value.

options: how many new users sign up
whether users keep coming back over time
questions.explanation: Retention is the truest test of value - whether people return.

options: the product itself to drive acquisition, conversion, and expansion
questions.explanation: In product-led growth the product does the selling, often through a free trial or tier.

lessons.title: What growth hacking is, and how it differs from marketing
lessons.grammar_note: Growth hacking is a repeatable process - hypothesis, test, measure - not a bag of one-off tricks; a tactic that worked elsewhere must still be tested on your own users.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what growth hacking is in plain terms, name the person who coined it, and say clearly how it differs from traditional marketing. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, who coined the phrase growth hacking, and what single goal did he place above everything else?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Growth hacking is a data-driven way of growing a product in which marketing, engineering, and product work as one team running many small, cheap experiments. The phrase was coined by Sean Ellis in 2010 to name a role whose single goal is growth, not awards or vanity. Traditional marketing usually focuses on the top of the funnel - awareness and acquisition - and often measures success loosely, over long campaigns, with large budgets. A growth hacker instead takes responsibility for the whole funnel, from the first visit to repeat use and word of mouth, and insists that every tactic be measurable. The method is a tight loop: form a clear hypothesis, build the smallest test that can prove or disprove it, measure the result honestly, then keep what works and discard what does not. Sean Ellis also warned against spending heavily on acquisition before a product has real demand, because paid growth on a weak product simply fills a leaky bucket faster. The mindset borrows from engineering: test, measure, iterate, rather than guess.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: A few famous stories show the mindset. Hotmail added one line to the bottom of every outgoing message, 'PS I love you. Get your free email', turning each user into a tiny billboard and reaching millions quickly. Dropbox offered extra free storage to both the person who referred a friend and the friend who joined, so growth paid for itself. Airbnb let hosts cross-post listings to other classified sites, borrowing an existing audience. Each example is cheap, built into the product, and measurable - the hallmarks of growth hacking. Contrast that with a traditional billboard campaign: expensive, hard to attribute, and disconnected from the product experience. Sean Ellis also popularized a simple test for product-market fit: ask users how they would feel if they could no longer use the product, and treat roughly forty percent answering 'very disappointed' as a green light to pour fuel on growth. The common thread is leverage - small, testable changes inside the product that compound, rather than one-off spends outside it.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In one sentence, how does growth hacking differ from traditional marketing? 2) Who coined the term, and in what year? 3) Why is paid acquisition risky before product-market fit? 4) What made the Hotmail signature line a growth hack rather than an ad? 5) What rough percentage of 'very disappointed' users suggests product-market fit? 6) Name one trait a growth hacker shares with an engineer. Answers: 1) Growth hacking runs fast, measurable experiments across the whole funnel, while traditional marketing often focuses on broad, loosely measured awareness at the top. 2) Sean Ellis, in 2010. 3) Because spending to acquire users for a product people do not value just drains money faster without lasting growth. 4) It was free, built into the product, and every message spread it, so it was cheap and measurable rather than a paid placement - the product did the marketing. 5) Around forty percent. 6) A habit of testing, measuring, and iterating rather than guessing.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating growth hacking as a bag of one-off tricks instead of a repeatable process of hypothesis, test, and measurement. Mistake: chasing growth before the product is worth keeping, which only speeds up churn. Mistake: copying another company's famous tactic without checking that it fits your own users and funnel - a trick that worked for a file-sharing tool may fall flat for a payments app. Remember that the goal is durable growth, not a momentary spike that fades once the trick stops working. Exit ticket: (a) Who coined the term growth hacking? (b) Which part of the funnel does a growth hacker own, compared with a traditional marketer? Answers: Sean Ellis; the growth hacker owns the whole funnel from first visit through repeat use and referral, while the traditional marketer typically owns only the top, acquisition and awareness.

lessons.title: The AARRR 'pirate metrics' funnel
lessons.grammar_note: AARRR is read like a pirate's growl, which is why it is nicknamed pirate metrics; the five letters are stages every user flows through, not a ranking.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name the five stages of the AARRR funnel in order, say what each one measures, and explain why viewing growth as a funnel helps you find the real bottleneck. Warm-up: if a hundred people visit your site and only two ever come back a week later, which stage is most likely broken?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The AARRR funnel, nicknamed pirate metrics, was popularized by the investor Dave McClure as a simple map of how users move through a product. Its five stages are Acquisition, how people first find you; Activation, their first genuinely good experience; Retention, whether they keep coming back; Referral, whether they tell other people; and Revenue, whether they pay. Reading the five letters top to bottom turns growth from a vague goal into a measurable pipeline. The key insight is that each stage has its own conversion rate - the share of users who make it to the next step - and that your growth is limited by the weakest stage, not the loudest one. A product can pour money into acquisition and still stall if activation is broken and new users never reach value. By attaching a number to each stage, you can compare them, spot the biggest drop-off, and fix the bottleneck that actually constrains growth. The funnel also keeps teams honest: a surge in signups looks great until you notice that retention a week later is near zero, which points straight at activation or product value rather than acquisition.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Suppose ten thousand people visit, which is acquisition. Two thousand create an account and complete a first key action, which is activation, a twenty percent activation rate. Of those, six hundred are still active after a week, which is retention. One hundred and twenty invite a friend, which is referral, and three hundred start paying, which is revenue. Laid out this way, the numbers tell a story: activation is leaking eighty percent of visitors, so improving the onboarding flow would likely help more than buying extra traffic. Compare two fixes. Doubling acquisition to twenty thousand visits, at the same rates, yields four thousand activated users - good, but you paid for every extra visit. Instead, lifting activation from twenty to thirty percent turns the original ten thousand visits into three thousand activated users for free. That is the power of reading the funnel: the cheapest win usually sits at the leakiest stage, not the top. Each stage suggests its own metric - cost per acquisition, activation rate, weekly retention, viral coefficient for referral, and average revenue per user for revenue.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) List the five AARRR stages in order. 2) What does activation measure? 3) If acquisition is strong but retention is near zero, which end of the funnel needs work? 4) With ten thousand visits and a twenty-five percent activation rate, how many users activate? 5) Why can improving a middle stage beat buying more traffic? 6) Which metric fits the referral stage? Answers: 1) Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue. 2) Whether a new user reaches a first genuinely valuable experience. 3) The lower middle - activation and retention - not acquisition, since people are arriving but not staying. 4) Two thousand five hundred users. 5) Because a higher conversion rate multiplies every visit you already pay for, often at no extra acquisition cost. 6) The viral coefficient, the average number of new users each existing user brings.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: obsessing over acquisition while ignoring the stages below it, so you pay to fill a leaky bucket. Mistake: celebrating vanity totals like raw signups instead of stage-by-stage conversion rates. Mistake: treating the five stages as a strict ranking rather than a pipeline every user flows through; in reality a user can move through all five, and your job is to measure each transition. Exit ticket: (a) What do the five letters of AARRR stand for? (b) Why does the weakest stage, not the biggest, limit growth? Answers: Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue; because every user must pass through each stage in turn, so the stage with the worst conversion rate caps how many reach the bottom, no matter how large the top is.

lessons.title: Running growth experiments, A/B tests, and the north-star metric
lessons.grammar_note: A hypothesis is a testable guess written as 'if we change X, then metric Y will move, because Z' - if you cannot measure Y, it is not yet a hypothesis.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Run a growth experiment through its four steps - ideate, prioritize, test, analyze - design a clean A/B test, and choose a north-star metric. Warm-up: if you have forty growth ideas but time to test only three this month, what do you need before you can choose which three?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Growth hacking turns growth into a repeatable loop with four steps. First you ideate: gather many ideas for moving a target metric. Next you prioritize, because you can never test everything at once; teams often score each idea by expected impact, confidence that it will work, and ease of running it, then test the top scorers first. Then you test, usually by changing one thing and measuring the effect, most often with an A/B test. Finally you analyze: did the metric move, and was the change large enough to be real rather than random noise? Whatever you learn - win, loss, or surprise - feeds the next round of ideas. The loop only works if the whole team agrees on one guiding number, the north-star metric. A north-star metric is the single measure that best captures the value users get from the product, such as nights booked, messages sent, or weekly active users. A good one predicts long-term growth, so moving it moves the business, while a vanity metric like raw page views can rise even as real value falls.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: An A/B test splits users at random into two groups. The control group sees the current version; the variant group sees one change, such as a new signup button or headline. Because assignment is random, any difference in behavior can be attributed to the change rather than to the kind of person in each group. Suppose the control converts at ten percent and the variant at twelve percent. That looks like a win, but you must check whether the gap is statistically significant - likely real rather than chance - which depends on how many users you tested. A two-point lift seen across fifty users means little; the same lift across fifty thousand users is convincing. Change one thing at a time, or you will not know which change caused the result. For prioritizing, a simple scoring method combines impact, confidence, and ease, so a quick, high-confidence, high-impact idea beats a slow, uncertain one. The north-star ties it together: every test should aim to move that one number, so wins add up instead of pulling in different directions.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the four steps of the growth experiment loop. 2) In an A/B test, what does the control group see? 3) Why change only one thing per test? 4) Control converts at eight percent, variant at nine percent, but only thirty users saw each - should you trust it? 5) Give a north-star metric for a messaging app. 6) Why prioritize at all? Answers: 1) Ideate, prioritize, test, analyze. 2) The existing, unchanged version, used as a baseline for comparison. 3) So you can tell which change caused any difference in the result. 4) No - the sample is far too small for the gap to be statistically significant, so it could easily be chance. 5) Messages sent per active user, or weekly active users, since those capture real value. 6) Because you can never test every idea at once, so you spend limited time on the ideas most likely to move the metric.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: changing several things in one test, so a win cannot be traced to a cause. Mistake: calling a result a win on a tiny sample, before it is statistically significant. Mistake: picking a vanity north-star like total page views that can climb while real value drops. Mistake: running tests with no shared target, so wins on different screens cancel out. Exit ticket: (a) What are the four steps of the loop? (b) What makes a metric a good north-star? Answers: ideate, prioritize, test, analyze; a good north-star captures the core value users get and predicts long-term growth, so moving it reliably grows the business rather than flattering a report.

questions.prompt: The clearest difference between growth hacking and traditional marketing is that growth hacking...
options: emphasizes rapid, measurable experiments across the whole funnel
questions.explanation: Growth hacking owns the whole funnel with fast, measurable experiments.

questions.prompt: The five stages of AARRR, in order, are...
questions.explanation: Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue - the pirate-metrics order.

questions.prompt: In the growth experiment loop, what comes right after you prioritize ideas?
questions.explanation: The loop is ideate, prioritize, test, analyze - testing follows prioritizing.

questions.prompt: A good growth hypothesis should be...
options: specific and measurable, so the test can confirm or reject it
questions.explanation: If you cannot measure the predicted outcome, it is not yet a usable hypothesis.

options: track vanity numbers like raw page views
reflect the core value users get and predict long-term growth
be kept secret from the team
questions.explanation: The north-star captures delivered value, so moving it moves the business.

questions.prompt: In an A/B test, checking statistical significance helps you...
options: decide whether a difference is likely real rather than random noise
pick the prettier design regardless of data
questions.explanation: Significance tells you whether the measured gap is likely real given the sample size.

lessons.title: Acquisition channels
lessons.grammar_note: A channel is worth keeping only when the value of the users it brings is higher than the cost of acquiring them - compare lifetime value against cost per acquisition.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: List the main acquisition channels, tell paid from organic, and judge a channel by comparing what a user is worth against what they cost. Warm-up: a channel brings users for five dollars each, but each user is only ever worth three dollars - should you keep spending on it?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Acquisition is the top of the funnel: how strangers first find your product. Channels fall into a few families. Organic search brings people who find you through unpaid search results, which rewards useful content and a healthy site. Paid advertising buys attention on search engines and social platforms, giving fast but rented traffic that stops the moment you stop paying. Content marketing earns trust and search traffic over time through articles, videos, and guides. Social and community channels spread word of mouth. Partnerships and integrations borrow another company's audience. Outbound sales and cold outreach target specific buyers directly. Two numbers decide whether a channel is worth it. Cost per acquisition, or CPA, is what you pay on average to gain one user. Customer lifetime value, or LTV, is the total value that user brings over time. A channel is healthy only when LTV comfortably exceeds CPA; a common rule of thumb is that lifetime value should be at least three times the cost to acquire. Early on, most products rely on one or two channels that fit them, not all of them at once.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Imagine two channels. Paid search costs you twenty dollars per new customer, and those customers are worth sixty dollars over their lifetime, a three-to-one ratio - healthy, and worth scaling. A second channel, a cheap social campaign, costs only four dollars per customer, but those users churn fast and are worth just six dollars, a weaker ratio once you account for the effort to run it. Cheaper per click is not always better. Organic and content channels behave differently: they cost time and effort up front and pay off slowly, but once an article ranks it can bring users for months at almost no extra cost, so the effective CPA keeps falling. Paid channels are the opposite - instant but rented. Many teams keep a list of roughly nineteen possible channels, run cheap tests on a few, double down on the one or two that work, and ignore the rest until the first ones saturate. Saturation matters: as you spend more on a paid channel, the cost per user usually rises, so a channel that looked great small can turn unprofitable at scale.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name three acquisition channels. 2) What does CPA stand for, and what does it measure? 3) If LTV is thirty dollars and CPA is forty dollars, is the channel healthy? 4) Why can an organic article's effective cost per user fall over time? 5) What happens to the cost per user as you pour more money into a paid channel? 6) Why focus on one or two channels early? Answers: 1) Any three of: organic search, paid advertising, content marketing, social, partnerships, outbound sales. 2) Cost per acquisition - the average amount you pay to gain one new user. 3) No - you spend more to acquire a user than the user is worth, so you lose money on each one. 4) Because the article keeps bringing users for months at little extra cost, spreading its fixed effort over more and more people. 5) It usually rises, as the channel saturates and cheap attention runs out. 6) Because a small team cannot run every channel well, so it is better to win one that fits than to spread thin across all of them.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: judging a channel by cost per click instead of by lifetime value against cost per acquisition. Mistake: assuming a paid channel that works at small spend will stay cheap as you scale, when saturation drives the cost up. Mistake: spreading a small team across every channel at once rather than winning one that fits. Mistake: forgetting that paid traffic stops the instant the budget does, while organic keeps working. Exit ticket: (a) What two numbers tell you whether a channel is worth keeping? (b) Name one paid and one organic channel. Answers: customer lifetime value and cost per acquisition, with LTV needing to exceed CPA; a paid channel such as search or social ads, and an organic channel such as content marketing or organic search.

lessons.title: Viral loops, referral programs, and the viral coefficient
lessons.grammar_note: The viral coefficient, often written k, is invites sent per user times the share of invites that convert - above one means self-sustaining growth, below one means every cohort shrinks.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain a viral loop, design a referral program, and compute a viral coefficient to tell self-sustaining growth from a boost that fades. Warm-up: if each user invites four friends and one in four accepts, does the user base grow on its own?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A viral loop is a cycle in which using a product leads existing users to bring in new users, who then do the same. The strength of the loop is captured by the viral coefficient, often written k. It equals the average number of invites each user sends multiplied by the share of those invites that convert into new users. If k is greater than one, each person brings on average more than one new person, and the user base grows on its own, cohort after cohort. If k is below one, invitations still help, but each wave is smaller than the last, so growth fades without fresh outside acquisition. Even a k below one is valuable, because it lowers your effective cost of acquisition. Two kinds of virality exist. Inherent virality comes from products that are more useful when friends join, such as messaging or file sharing. Incentivized virality is a referral program that rewards sharing, like giving both sides a bonus. Loop speed matters too: a loop that completes in a day compounds far faster than one that takes a month, even at the same k.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Compute k with a worked case. Say each user sends four invites and one in four accepts. Then k equals four times one quarter, which is one. A k of exactly one means each cohort replaces itself - steady, not explosive. Lift acceptance to one in two and k becomes two: each user brings two more, who bring four, then eight, and growth compounds. Now a referral program: Dropbox gave free storage to both the referrer and the new user, which raised both the number of invites sent and the rate they converted, because the reward felt fair to each side. Good programs reward both sides, make sharing effortless, and place the prompt at a moment of delight, such as right after a user succeeds at something. Cycle time is the quiet multiplier: with the same k above one, halving the time a loop takes roughly doubles how fast you grow. Beware fake virality - buying invite lists or nagging users - which inflates invites sent but not genuine conversions, and often annoys people enough to hurt retention.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Write the formula for the viral coefficient k. 2) Each user sends five invites and one in five converts - what is k, and does the base grow on its own? 3) Why is a referral that rewards both sides usually stronger? 4) Why does loop cycle time matter even when k is fixed? 5) Is a k of 0.6 useless? 6) What value of k marks self-sustaining growth? Answers: 1) k equals invites sent per user times the share of invites that convert. 2) k equals five times one fifth, which is one, so the base holds steady rather than growing on its own. 3) Because rewarding both the referrer and the new user raises both the number of invites and their conversion rate, and feels fair. 4) A shorter cycle completes more loops in the same period, so growth compounds faster at the same k. 5) No - a k below one still lowers your effective acquisition cost, even though each cohort is smaller than the last. 6) Any k greater than one.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing invites sent with real conversions, so a loud but low-converting campaign looks viral when it is not. Mistake: rewarding only the referrer, which feels one-sided and converts worse than rewarding both parties. Mistake: ignoring cycle time and assuming two products with the same k grow equally fast. Mistake: forcing virality through spam, which inflates vanity numbers while driving away the users you have. Exit ticket: (a) What does a viral coefficient above one mean? (b) What two quantities multiply to give k? Answers: that each existing user brings on average more than one new user, so the user base grows on its own; the average invites sent per user and the share of those invites that convert into new users.

lessons.title: Activation, onboarding, retention, and engagement
lessons.grammar_note: Activation is the first time a user reaches real value; retention is whether they keep coming back - onboarding drives the first, while ongoing value and habit drive the second.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define activation and retention, design onboarding that gets users to first value fast, and read a retention curve to judge engagement. Warm-up: a photo app has huge signups but almost no one opens it a week later - is the problem activation, retention, or both?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Activation is the moment a new user first experiences the product's real value - the 'aha' moment. For a file tool it might be uploading a first file; for a social app, following enough people to see a lively feed. Onboarding is the guided path that carries a brand-new user to that moment as quickly and smoothly as possible, removing every needless step. Retention is whether users keep coming back over time, and it is the truest test of value: a product people return to has something worth returning for. Engagement describes how deeply and how often active users use the product between visits. These stages are linked. Weak onboarding means users never activate, and users who never reach value almost never retain. Strong activation sets up retention but does not guarantee it - the product must keep delivering value and, ideally, build a habit tied to a regular trigger. Many teams define activation as a concrete first action taken within a set time, such as inviting a teammate in the first week, because that action reliably predicts whether the user will stick around.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Retention is usually read as a curve: of the users who joined in a given week, what share are still active one week later, two weeks later, and so on. A healthy product's curve drops at first, then flattens into a plateau - a core group that keeps coming back. A curve that falls to near zero means the product is not yet worth returning to, no matter how good acquisition looks. Famous activation targets make this concrete: early teams found that users who connected with enough friends in their first days, or who took one key action quickly, retained far better, so onboarding was redesigned to push everyone toward that action. Good onboarding strips steps, shows value before asking for commitment, and uses empty states, checklists, and gentle prompts to guide the first session. Engagement is deepened with habit triggers - a timely message, a streak, a useful summary - that give users a reason to return. The order matters: fix activation before pouring money into acquisition, because sending more people into a product they never activate on only wastes the spend.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is activation? 2) What is the job of onboarding? 3) What does a retention curve that flattens into a plateau tell you? 4) If signups are high but week-one retention is near zero, what should you fix first? 5) Give an example activation action for a team chat tool. 6) Why fix activation before scaling acquisition? Answers: 1) The first time a new user reaches the product's real value, the aha moment. 2) To carry a brand-new user to that first value as fast and smoothly as possible, cutting needless steps. 3) That a core group finds lasting value and keeps returning - a sign of real product-market fit. 4) Activation and onboarding, since people arrive but never reach value; buying more traffic first would waste money. 5) Inviting a teammate, or sending a first message, within the first week. 6) Because more users poured into a product they do not activate on simply leak out, wasting the acquisition spend.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: measuring signups as success while ignoring whether users ever reach value. Mistake: cramming onboarding with tours and forms that delay the first real win. Mistake: judging retention from a single day instead of a curve that shows whether it plateaus. Mistake: spending on acquisition while activation is broken, which only speeds the leak. Exit ticket: (a) What is the difference between activation and retention? (b) What shape of retention curve signals a healthy product? Answers: activation is a user reaching first real value, while retention is whether users keep coming back over time; a healthy curve drops at first and then flattens into a plateau, showing a stable core of returning users rather than falling to zero.

lessons.title: Product-led growth, ethics, and the limits of growth tactics
lessons.grammar_note: A growth tactic is sustainable only if it would still look fair once the user understands exactly what it is doing - tricks win a click and lose the trust that drives retention and referral.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain product-led growth, weigh the ethics of growth tactics, and name the limits where aggressive tactics backfire. Warm-up: a signup flow hides the cancel button and pre-checks a paid upgrade - it lifts short-term revenue, so why might it hurt growth overall?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Product-led growth, often shortened to PLG, is a strategy in which the product itself drives acquisition, conversion, and expansion, rather than a large sales team. A free trial or free tier lets users experience value before paying; the product guides them to upgrade when they hit a natural limit. Built-in sharing turns users into a channel. PLG works best when the product delivers value quickly and clearly, so it leans heavily on strong activation and onboarding. But growth tactics have an ethical edge. A dark pattern is a design that tricks users into actions they would not freely choose - hidden cancel buttons, pre-checked upsells, fake scarcity, or guilt-worded decline links. Such tricks can lift a short-term number, yet they erode trust, and trust is what drives retention, word of mouth, and the very referrals a healthy funnel depends on. The limits of growth hacking are real: no clever tactic rescues a product people do not value, data must be handled lawfully and with consent, and a spike bought by annoying people usually reverses. The durable version of growth is honest value, delivered well.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Classic PLG examples include tools that spread inside a company as one team invites another, or free tiers generous enough to hook users who later pay for more capacity. The upgrade prompt appears exactly when the user feels the limit, so paying feels like a natural next step rather than a sales pitch. Contrast that with dark patterns. A pre-checked box that adds a paid add-on may raise revenue this quarter, but refunds, chargebacks, angry reviews, and lost referrals often erase the gain and then some. Fake countdown timers and invented low-stock warnings can nudge a purchase once, but when users notice the timer resets, trust collapses. The practical test is simple: would the tactic still look fair if you explained it plainly to the user? Honest urgency - a genuine deadline - passes; a fabricated one does not. Growth also has structural limits. If a product has no real demand, every channel and loop just leaks faster. If acquisition cost exceeds lifetime value, scaling loses more money the bigger it gets. And privacy law and platform rules cap how aggressively you may collect data or send messages.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In one sentence, what is product-led growth? 2) Give one example of a dark pattern. 3) Why can a dark pattern that raises revenue still hurt growth overall? 4) What simple test separates honest urgency from a manipulative trick? 5) Name one structural limit that no tactic can overcome. 6) Why does PLG depend so heavily on activation? Answers: 1) A strategy where the product itself drives acquisition, conversion, and expansion, often through a free trial or tier and built-in sharing. 2) A hidden cancel button, a pre-checked paid upsell, or a fake countdown timer. 3) Because it erodes the trust that drives retention, word of mouth, and referrals, so refunds and lost goodwill often outweigh the short-term gain. 4) Whether the tactic would still look fair once you explained it plainly to the user. 5) A product with no real demand, or a cost per acquisition higher than lifetime value - no tactic fixes either. 6) Because without a sales team to persuade users, the product must get them to real value by itself, fast.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating product-led growth as 'build it and they will come', when it still demands strong onboarding and a clear path to value. Mistake: reaching for dark patterns to hit a quarterly number, trading durable trust for a reversible spike. Mistake: assuming any tactic can rescue a product people do not want. Mistake: ignoring privacy law and platform rules until they halt your growth. Exit ticket: (a) What drives acquisition and expansion in product-led growth? (b) Why do dark patterns tend to backfire over time? Answers: the product itself, through free access, fast value, and built-in sharing, rather than a large sales team; because they erode user trust, and trust is what powers retention, referrals, and word of mouth, so the short-term gain reverses as users leave and warn others.

items.translation: a data-driven practice of growing a product through fast, cheap, measurable experiments across the whole funnel
items.example: The team treated growth hacking as a loop: hypothesis, test, measure, repeat.

items.translation: the pirate-metrics funnel of Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, and Revenue
items.example: Mapping the AARRR funnel showed that activation, not acquisition, was the bottleneck.

items.translation: the average number of new users each existing user brings; above one means self-sustaining growth
items.example: With four invites per user and a one-in-four conversion, the viral coefficient was exactly one.

items.translation: the moment a new user first experiences the product's real value, the aha moment
items.example: They defined activation as uploading a first file within the opening session.

items.translation: the share of users who keep coming back over a given period
items.example: A retention curve that flattens into a plateau signals a healthy, sticky product.

items.translation: the rate at which users stop using or cancel the product
items.example: High churn meant every new signup was quietly offset by a departing user.

items.translation: the single number that best captures the value a product delivers and predicts long-term growth
items.example: Messages sent per active user became the north-star metric the whole team rallied behind.

items.translation: a strategy where the product itself drives acquisition, conversion, and expansion, often via a free tier
items.example: Product-led growth let the free plan do the selling before any salesperson got involved.
